topic.title: The giveaway that farms you
topic.claim: The iPhone giveaway asking you to follow, tag and share isn't generosity; you're the unpaid growth team.
topic.moment: You tag three friends under a giveaway reel, and so do forty thousand strangers.

turn.believed: A creator is giving away a phone to thank their followers.
turn.actually: One phone buys them tens of thousands of new follows, tags and shares, which is cheaper than any ad.

topic.because: Each entry rule converts you into free reach. The prize is a tiny cost against the followers and spread it manufactures in a week.
topic.payoff: The giveaway where you do all the sharing is the ad where you're the medium.
topic.behaviour: Accounts run follow-tag-share giveaways to cheaply buy reach and followers.
topic.mechanism: Each entry rule turns followers into free distribution worth more than the prize.
topic.send_to: the friend who tags you in every giveaway
topic.why_now: Festive-season giveaways are everywhere right now.

cover.headline: That iPhone giveaway made you [its unpaid growth team]
cover.sub: You entered to win a phone. You ended up doing the marketing.

paragraphs:
That iPhone giveaway looks like a thank-you to followers. Your follow, your tags and your story share are what it's really collecting.
Swipe to read →
slides.why_swipe: What exactly is a giveaway collecting from the people who enter?

paragraphs: It's festive season and a reel stops your thumb. A new iPhone, still sealed in the box, and a creator smiling into the camera. "This one's for my amazing family!"
The rules sit in the caption. Follow, like, tag three friends, share it to your story.
slides.why_swipe: What does the reader do next, and who else is doing it?

paragraphs: So you follow. You tag the friend who always replies, the one who never does, and a college batchmate just to make it three.
Then you open the comments. Thousands of strangers, three names each, the same small chore done over and over.
You share it to your story because the caption said so, and go back to scrolling.
slides.why_swipe: It felt like nothing. So what did all those small steps actually do?

paragraphs: But look at what each rule leaves behind. The follow stays long after the reel is forgotten. Each tag lands in three people's notifications, from a name they recognise.
Your story share puts the reel in front of your circle, people who would never have found that account on their own.
**Add up every entry and the phone starts to look like the cheap part.**
slides.why_swipe: Is it all a trick, or does someone actually get the phone?

paragraphs: And yes, a real person gets a real phone. Somewhere a stranger opens a DM and screams, and that part is genuine.
It's one person, though. Everyone else in those comments did the same work for the same week and got a story view count.
You were never really a contestant. You were the medium the ad ran on.
slides.why_swipe: So what's left on the reader's side once it's over?

paragraphs: Think back to the last giveaway you entered.
That account still turns up in your feed. The winner's name never did.
**But you still remember the batchmate you tagged just to make it three.**

end.save: Read it again before you tag three friends under the next festive giveaway.
end.send: Send it to the friend who tags you in every giveaway.
end.promise: How the internet sells to you.

draft.caption: Who won the last giveaway you entered? And who did you tag just to make it three?
draft.alt_text: Carousel post. The cover reads: That iPhone giveaway made you its unpaid growth team. The slides follow you through a festive iPhone giveaway reel. You follow the account, tag three friends including a college batchmate just to make it three, see thousands of strangers in the comments doing the same, and share it to your story. The next slide shows what each rule leaves behind: the follow stays, each tag lands in three people's notifications, and the story share puts the reel in front of your circle, so the phone starts to look like the cheap part. It admits a real person does win a real phone, but everyone else did the same work for nothing, which makes you the medium the ad ran on rather than a contestant. It closes by asking you to think of the last giveaway you entered: the account still shows up in your feed, you never learned the winner's name, but you still remember the batchmate you tagged to make it three.
